Neural Signaling
MED 808: Neuroscience, Neuroanatomy, and Neurology (NNN); Fall 2026

Larry D. Alexander, Ph. D.

1

Learning Objectives
After studying this lecture, the student should be able to:
1. Classify nerve fibers by conduction velocity, diameter, and myelination, and
explain how these properties affect signal transmission.
2. Identify the types of sensory receptors and explain how excitation of a sensory
nerve fiber by a receptor potential produced in a Pacinian corpuscle or Rod cell
generates a receptor potential.
3. Describe how different types of sensory receptors transduce external stimuli
into neural signals, including key mechanisms of receptor activation.
4. Explain the concept of sensory adaptation and its physiological significance in
normal perception and clinical conditions.
2

Lecture Outline
I. Types of Nerve Fibers
II. Sensory Reception
III. Sensory Transduction and Receptor Potentials
IV. Types of Sensory Receptors and Their
Transduction Mechanisms
V. Sensory Adaptation
3

Types of Nerve
Fibers
4

Overview of Nerve Fibers
• Nerve fibers are the axons of neurons that carry electrical impulses.
• Sensory and Motor Nerve Fibers
– Sensory Fibers (Afferent): Transmit sensory information from receptors
(e.g., touch, pain, proprioception) to the CNS
– Motor Fibers (Efferent): Carry motor commands from the CNS to
muscles and glands for actions (voluntary and involuntary)
• Nerve fibers differ in diameter, conduction velocity, and function.
5

Nerve Fiber Classification, Cont.
• Based on Diameter and Conduction Velocity:
– A fibers (myelinated, fast- to medium- conducting)
– B fibers (moderately myelinated, slower-conducting)
– C fibers (unmyelinated, slow-conducting)
• Based on Function:
– Sensory fibers (afferent)
– Motor fibers (efferent)
– Autonomic fibers (sympathetic and parasympathetic)
6

A Fibers
• A Fibers: Myelinated
• Types of A fibers:
– Aα (alpha): Motor fibers for muscle control and proprioception; (large-diameter); fast
conducting
– Aβ (beta): Sensory fibers for touch, pressure, and vibration; (large-diameter); fast
conducting
– Aγ (gamma): Motor fibers for muscle spindles (regulating muscle tone); (medium-
diameter); medium conducting
– Aδ (delta): Sensory fibers for touch, pressure, fast pain, and temperature (e.g., cold);
(small-diameter); medium conducting
• Conduction Velocity: 80-120 m/sec (Aα) to 5-30 m/sec (Aδ).
7

B Fibers
• B Fibers: Myelinated, Slower Conduction
– Found mainly in the autonomic nervous system (e.g., preganglionic
autonomic nerves)
– Carry signals from the CNS to autonomic ganglia (preganglionic
fibers)
– Conduction velocity is slower than A fibers (3-15 m/sec)
– Control smooth muscle activity, heart rate, and glandular function
8

C Fibers
• C Fibers: Unmyelinated, Slow-Conducting, Found mainly in
the autonomic nervous system
– Small diameter and lack of myelination lead to slow conduction (0.5-
2 m/sec)
– Involved in transmitting slow, chronic pain and temperature
sensations
– C fibers are also part of the autonomic nervous system (e.g.,
postganglionic autonomic fibers)
– Function in long-lasting dull pain and visceral sensations
9

Conduction Velocity and Myelination
• The Role of Myelination in Nerve Conduction
– Myelination speeds up signal transmission
• Increases membrane resistance and lowers capacitance
– Myelinated fibers (A and B) use saltatory conduction, where
the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier
– Unmyelinated fibers (C) conduct more slowly due to
continuous conduction
10

Conduction Velocity and Myelination,
Cont.
• An axon’s myelin sheath is not continuous.
• Every 1 to 2 mm is a 2- to 3-μm segment of exposed axonal
membrane known as a node of Ranvier.
• Nodes are tightly packed with Na+ channels, whereas the
internodal regions (areas lying hidden beneath the myelin
sheath) have virtually no channels.
• In practice, this means that an action potential leapfrogs
from one node to the next down the length of the axon,
a behavior known as nodal, or saltatory conduction.
• Breaks in the myelin sheath occur at the nodes of
Ranvier.
Figure 5.2 Neuronal anatomy. (Adopted from Lippincott
Illustrated Reviews Physiology, 3rd Ed.)
11

Conduction Velocity and Myelination,
Cont.
• Breaks in the myelin sheath occur at the
nodes of Ranvier.
Figure 5.4 Myelin and diameter effects on axonal conduction
velocity. (Adopted from Lippincott Illustrated Reviews
Physiology, 3rd Ed.)
12

Axonal Diameter and Conduction Velocity
• The Role of Myelination in Nerve Conduction
– Myelination speeds up signal transmission
• Increases membrane resistance and lowers capacitance
– Myelinated fibers (A and B) use saltatory conduction, where
the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier
– Unmyelinated fibers (C) conduct more slowly due to
continuous conduction
13

14

Clinical Relevance
• Disorders Related to Nerve Fibers
– Peripheral Neuropathy: Damage to peripheral nerves
affecting sensory and motor functions.
– Multiple Sclerosis: Damage to the myelin sheath of A and B
fibers leading to impaired transmission.
– Diabetic Neuropathy: Affects C fibers, causing chronic pain
and loss of sensation.
15

Summary of Nerve Fiber Types
• Nerve fibers in the peripheral nervous system are classified according to
their diameter.
• This is closely linked to the speed with which impulses spread along them
(i.e., their conduction velocity, and allows fibers to be crudely
characterized as to function.
• The fastest fibers are the myelinated large-diameter neurons (Aα).
• The slowest fibers are unmyelinated small (C) fibers
– Transmit pain impulses
16

Sensory Reception
17

Types of Sensory Receptors
• Sensory receptors are specialized cells or structures that transduce environmental energy
into electrical signals. They are classified by modality (type of stimulus detected):
– Mechanoreceptors – respond to mechanical deformation (touch, pressure, vibration, stretch)
• Examples: Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner’s corpuscles, hair cells in cochlea
– Thermoreceptors – detect temperature (warm/cold receptors in skin)
– Nociceptors – pain receptors; detect tissue damage (mechanical, thermal, chemical)
– Photoreceptors – detect light (rods and cones in retina)
– Chemoreceptors – detect chemicals (taste buds, olfactory receptors, carotid body)
– Electromagnetic receptors – specialized type (photoreceptors fall here)
– Proprioceptors – detect body position and movement (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs)
18

Mechanoreceptors: Sensing Touch and Pressure
• Found in the skin and other organs.
• Activated by pressure or changes in pressure.
• The physical deformation of the receptor membrane opens ion channels.
• Example: Pacinian corpuscles in subcutaneous tissue respond to deep
pressure; Meissner corpuscles in nonhairy skin (touch), baroreceptors
in the carotid sinus (blood pressure), hair cells on the organ of Corti
(audition) and in the semicircular canals (vestibular system).
• Once activated, the receptor generates an action potential that travels to
the brain.
19

Thermoreceptors: Detecting Temperature
• Found in the skin.
• Activated by temperature or changes in temperature
(detecting hot and cold stimuli).
• Specific receptors (e.g., TRPV1 for heat and TRPM8 for cold).
• Receptors activate ion channels, generating action potentials.
• Signals are transmitted to the brain where temperature
changes are perceived.
20

Nociceptors: Pain Receptors
• Activated by extremes of pressure, temperature, or
noxious chemicals.
• Activation leads to pain sensation to protect the body from
injury.
• Nociceptors generate action potentials that travel to the
spinal cord and brain.
• Chronic pain involves long-term activation of nociceptors.
21

Photoreceptors: Light Detection and Vision
• Located in the retina (rods and cones).
• Activated by light and are involved in vision.
• Rods detect low light, while cones detect color.
• Phototransduction: Light is absorbed, causing a change
in retinal pigment.
• This change activates a signal cascade leading to action
potentials sent to the visual cortex.
22

Chemoreceptors: Sensing Chemicals (Taste & Smell)
• Activated by chemical stimuli like taste (gustation) and smell
(olfaction)
– Gustatory cells in taste buds respond to specific chemicals (e.g.,
salty, sweet)
– Olfactory receptors detect airborne molecules and send signals to
the brain
• Mechanism: Chemical binds to receptors, initiating signal
transduction pathways.
23

24

Disorders Involving Visceral Sensory Neurons
• Visceral pain syndromes
• Autonomic dysreflexia
• Conditions like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
• Impact on Homeostasis: Malfunctioning of visceral
sensory neurons can disrupt homeostasis and lead to
chronic disorders.
25

Sensory Transduction
and Receptor Potentials
26

Sensory Transduction
• Sensory Transduction: The process by which a sensory receptor
converts an external stimulus (e.g., mechanical, thermal,
chemical, or light energy) into an electrical signal that the nervous
system can interpret.
• Mechanism:
– Stimulus energy activates ion channels (directly or via second
messengers)
– This changes ion fluxes (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) across the receptor
membrane
27

Receptor Potentials
• The direct electrical result of sensory transduction.
• A graded, local change in membrane potential in the receptor cell
caused by the stimulus.
• Properties:
– Amplitude depends on stimulus strength
– Can be depolarizing (e.g., mechanoreceptors) or hyperpolarizing (e.g., rods in
the retina)
– If threshold is reached, the receptor potential initiates action potentials in the
afferent neuron (or regulates neurotransmitter release in secondary synaptic
pathways)
28

Figure. 3.5 Receptor potentials in sensory receptor cells. Receptor potentials may be
either depolarizing (shown) or hyperpolarizing (not shown). A, if a depolarizing receptor
potential does not bring the membrane potential to threshold, no action potential occurs. B, If
a depolarizing receptor potential brings the membrane to threshold, then an action potential
occurs in the sensory receptor.
29

Receptor Potentials, Cont.
• Key properties:
• Local and graded: confined to receptor membrane,
amplitude varies with stimulus
• Summation possible: multiple stimuli can add together
• Decremental: spreads passively and decreases with distance
• Threshold function: must reach a certain level at the trigger
zone to generate action potentials
30

Relationship Between the Two
• Sensory transduction is the biophysical/biochemical
process (converts stimulus energy → electrical change).
• Receptor potential is the product (the graded potential
generated by that process).
• Put another way:
– Transduction = cause (conversion of stimulus energy)
– Receptor potential = effect (graded electrical signal produced)
31

Example Pathways
• Pacinian Corpuscle (touch)
– Mechanical deformation → mechanosensitive Na⁺ channels open
(sensory transduction) → depolarizing receptor potential →
action potentials in afferent nerve
• Rod Photoreceptor (vision)
– Photon absorption → rhodopsin activates transducin → PDE lowers
cGMP → Na⁺ channels close (sensory transduction) →
hyperpolarizing receptor potential → reduced glutamate release to
bipolar cells
32

Receptor Potentials in Pacinian Corpuscle
• Pacinian Corpuscle
(mechanoreceptor)
– Structure: Onion-like
layers around a central
nerve ending.
– Stimulus: Vibration or
pressure compresses
the lamellae.
FIGURE 47-3. Excitation of a sensory nerve fiber by a
receptor potential produced in a Pacinian corpuscle.
(Adopted from Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical
Physiology, 13th ed.)
33

Receptor Potentials in Pacinian Corpuscle, Cont.
• Mechanism:
– Mechanical deformation (e.g., pressure) stretches
the nerve ending’s membrane
– This opens mechanosensitive Na⁺ channels.
– Na⁺ influx (through mechanically gated ion
channels)→ local graded depolarization (receptor
potential)
– If the receptor potential reaches threshold at the
first node of Ranvier, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
open
– Action potentials are generated and propagated FIGURE 47-3. Excitation of a sensory
along the sensory fiber nerve fiber by a receptor potential
produced in a Pacinian corpuscle.
• Key point: Pacinian corpuscles adapt rapidly
(Adopted from Guyton and Hall Textbook
(phasic receptor) → detect vibration and rapid

changes, not steady pressure.
34

Receptor Potentials in Rod Photoreceptor
• Rod Cell (photoreceptor)
– Structure: Outer segment
contains rhodopsin (light-
sensitive pigment).
– Stimulus: Light (photons).
Figure 51-7 Phototransduction in the outer segment of the
photoreceptor (rod or cone) membrane. Adopted from Guyton
and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 13th ed.
35

• Mechanism:
– Light activates rhodopsin → retinal changes
shape → activates transducin (G-protein)
– Transducin activates phosphodiesterase
(PDE), which decreases intracellular cGMP
– Low cGMP → closure of cGMP-gated
Na⁺/Ca²⁺ channels in the outer segment
membrane
– Na⁺ influx decreases → cell hyperpolarizes
(unlike most receptors, rods hyperpolarize to
stimulus)
– Hyperpolarization reduces glutamate release
at the synapse with bipolar cells
– This modulates activity of bipolar → ganglion
cells → optic nerve action potentials
• Key point: Rods and cones do not fire Figure 51-7 Phototransduction in the outer
action potentials; they use graded
segment of the photoreceptor (rod or cone)
potentials to regulate transmitter release.
membrane. Adopted from Guyton and Hall
Textbook of Medical Physiology, 13th ed.
36

• Sensory receptors transduce environmental stimuli into electrical signals.
• Pacinian corpuscle: mechanical stimulus → depolarizing receptor potential →
action potentials.
• Rod cell: light stimulus → hyperpolarizing receptor potential → decreased
neurotransmitter release → downstream action potentials in ganglion cells.
37

Types of Sensory
Receptors and Their
Transduction Mechanisms
38

Mechanoreceptors
• Modalities: Touch, vibration, pressure, proprioception, hearing, balance
• Stimulus: Mechanical deformation (stretch, vibration, movement of hair cells).
• Mechanism:
– Mechanical force opens mechanosensitive ion channels → Na⁺ or K⁺ influx
– Generates a depolarizing receptor potential
• Examples:
– Pacinian corpuscles: detect vibration/pressure via deformation of lamellae
– Hair cells (cochlea, vestibular system): bending of stereocilia opens tip-link gated K⁺
channels → depolarization
39

Thermoreceptors
• Stimulus: Temperature changes.
• Mechanism:
– Heat or cold alters the gating of transient receptor potential (TRP)
ion channels
– Ion flux (Na⁺/Ca²⁺) → depolarizing receptor potential
• Examples:
– TRPV1: activated by heat >43°C and capsaicin
– TRPM8: activated by cold and menthol
40

Nociceptors
• Modalities: Pain
• Stimulus: Mechanical, thermal, or chemical injury.
• Mechanism:
– Noxious stimuli activate ion channels (TRP family, acid-sensing
ion channels, ATP-sensitive channels)
– Depolarization generates action potentials in Aδ (fast pain) or C
fibers (slow pain)
41

Photoreceptors
• Modalities: Vision
• Stimulus: Light (photons).
• Mechanism:
– Photon absorption by rhodopsin (rods) or photopsins (cones) → activates
transducin (G-protein)
– Transducin activates PDE, reducing cGMP
– cGMP-gated Na⁺/Ca²⁺ channels close → membrane hyperpolarization
– This decreases glutamate release, modulating bipolar/ganglion cell activity
• Key point: Photoreceptors hyperpolarize (opposite to most receptors).
42

Chemoreceptors
1. Olfactory receptors (smell)
– Odorant molecules bind GPCRs in olfactory neurons
– Activates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP increase
– cAMP opens cation channels → depolarization
2. Taste receptors (gustation)
– Salt: Na⁺ influx directly through ENaC channels
– Sour: H⁺ entry blocks K⁺ channels, depolarizing cell
– Sweet, bitter, umami: GPCRs activate second messenger pathways →
depolarization and neurotransmitter release
43

Chemoreceptors, Cont..
3. Carotid body chemoreceptors
– Detect ↓O₂, ↑CO₂, ↓pH
– Ion channel modulation leads to depolarization and
neurotransmitter release onto afferent nerve endings
44

Proprioceptors
• Modalities: Muscle length, tension, position
• Stimulus: Stretch or tension in muscles/tendons.
• Mechanism:
– Muscle spindle stretch → opens stretch-sensitive ion channels in Ia
afferents
– Golgi tendon organ tension → activates mechanosensitive channels in Ib
afferents
– Leads to depolarizing receptor potentials → action potentials in afferent
fibers
45

Encoding Stimuli into Neural Signals
• Amplitude of receptor potential = proportional to stimulus
intensity.
• If threshold reached: frequency of action potentials encodes
intensity.
• Adaptation:
– Phasic receptors (e.g., Pacinian corpuscle): rapid adaptation →
detect change.
– Tonic receptors (e.g., muscle spindle): slow adaptation → detect
sustained input.
46

Summary
• Different sensory receptors transduce stimuli by ion channel
modulation:
– Mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, nociceptors → direct ion channel
opening (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺)
– Photoreceptors → GPCR cascade → closure of cGMP-gated channels →
hyperpolarization
– Chemoreceptors → GPCRs or direct ion channel modulation → depolarization.
– Proprioceptors → mechanosensitive ion channels in muscle spindle or Golgi
tendon organs
• All lead to a receptor potential, which, if large enough, drives action
potential firing in sensory nerves or modulates neurotransmitter release.
47

Sensory Adaptation
48

Sensory Adaptation
• Sensory adaptation is the process by which sensory
receptors decrease their responsiveness during a
constant or unchanging stimulus
– The receptor potential amplitude diminishes → fewer action
potentials generated in the afferent nerve
– This prevents the nervous system from being overloaded with
redundant information
49

Types of Sensory Adaptation
• Rapidly Adapting (Phasic) Receptors
– Respond strongly at the onset and offset of a stimulus
– Stop firing during constant stimulation
– Detect changes, vibration, and movement
– Examples: Pacinian corpuscles (vibration), Meissner’s corpuscles (touch)
• Slowly Adapting (Tonic) Receptors
– Continue firing as long as the stimulus persists
– Encode duration and intensity of the stimulus
– Examples: Merkel cells (touch/pressure), muscle spindles (stretch), nociceptors
(pain)
50

Physiological Mechanisms
• Ion channel inactivation: sustained stimulation causes receptor ion
channels to gradually close (e.g., mechanosensitive Na⁺ channels).
• Receptor membrane properties: viscoelastic deformation in
mechanoreceptors (Pacinian corpuscle “slips” under constant pressure).
• Synaptic adaptation: in sensory pathways (e.g., decreased
neurotransmitter release in olfactory neurons with continuous odor
exposure).
• Central adaptation: modulation in higher CNS centers can also “tune
down” repetitive signals.
51

Physiological Significance
1. Efficiency of perception
– Frees the brain from constant background noise
– Enhances sensitivity to new or changing stimuli (e.g., detecting sudden movement in
vision or vibration in touch)
2. Special senses examples
– Vision: retinal photoreceptors adapt to light levels (dark vs light adaptation)
– Smell (olfaction): rapid adaptation prevents sensory overload in strong odors
– Touch: you stop feeling your clothes after a while (Pacinian corpuscle adaptation)
3. Homeostasis
– Prevents overstimulation by constant input, conserving energy for meaningful changes
52

Clinical Significance
1. Loss of adaptation
– Neuropathy (e.g., diabetic neuropathy): abnormal adaptation may impair
detection of vibrations or changes in pressure, predisposing to foot ulcers
– Chronic pain syndromes: nociceptors normally adapt slowly, but in neuropathic
pain, adaptation fails → persistent, exaggerated pain sensation (hyperalgesia)
2. Abnormal hypersensitivity
– Tinnitus: failure of auditory adaptation in cochlear or central circuits leads to
persistent perception of sound
– Allodynia: normally non-painful stimuli perceived as painful due to altered
central adaptation
53

Clinical Significance, Cont.
3. Deficits in sensory adaptation
– Olfactory loss (anosmia/hyposmia): impaired adaptation can
affect appetite, safety (e.g., failure to detect smoke or gas)
– Autism spectrum disorders: atypical sensory adaptation →
hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory input
54

Summary
• Sensory adaptation: reduction in receptor response during
sustained stimulation.
• Rapid (phasic) receptors → detect changes; slow (tonic)
receptors → encode duration/intensity.
• Physiological importance: filters redundant signals, emphasizes
new information.
• Clinical relevance: disrupted adaptation contributes to pain
syndromes, sensory neuropathies, tinnitus, and sensory processing
disorders.

Spinal Cord
Clinical Correlates

Brown Séquard Syndrome (Hemisection)
Cause: Spinal cord hemisection; classically penetrating trauma
At the Lesion
• Ipsilateral LMN signs (anterior horn)
• Ipsilateral complete sensory loss at lesion level
Below the Lesion
• Ipsilateral UMN signs (corticospinal tract)
• Ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, proprioception (dorsal column)
• Contralateral loss of pain, temperature (spinothalamic tract)
CST + DCML = ipsilateral | Spinothalamic = contralateral
Last, 12e.

Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA) Syndrome
Cause
• Infarction of anterior 2/3 of spinal cord
• May occur with aortic pathology or surgery, ASA occlusion
Below the Lesion
• Bilateral UMN weakness (corticospinal tracts)
• Bilateral loss of pain, temperature (spinothalamic tracts)
• Vibration, proprioception, fine touch preserved (dorsal column spared)
• ± Autonomic dysfunction (bladder, bowel, sexual, hypotension)
At the Lesion Level
• LMN weakness (anterior horn)
Last, 12e.

Artery of Adamkiewicz
• Major segmental medullary artery
• Reinforces blood supply to the lower spinal cord
• Usually arises from the lower thoracic/upper lumbar region (T9–L2)
• Injury during aortic surgery may cause anterior spinal artery syndrome
Arterial Supply of Spinal Cord
Fig. 2.55. GAS, 5e.

Syringomyelia
• Fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the central spinal cord
• Most commonly affects cervical cord
• Damages crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure
• → Bilateral pain/temperature loss in a cape-like distribution
• Vibration/proprioception preserved
With expansion
• Anterior horn → LMN weakness/hand muscle atrophy
• Lateral horn/sympathetic pathway → Horner syndrome
• Corticospinal tract → UMN signs below lesion
Association
• Chiari I malformation
Last, 12e.

Subacute Combined Degeneration
• Associated with vitamin B12 deficiency
• Demyelination of:
• Dorsal columns
• Lateral corticospinal tracts
• ↓ Vibration, proprioception → sensory ataxia, positive Romberg
• Corticospinal involvement → spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski
• May cause paresthesias and peripheral neuropathy
B12 deficiency → dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts
Last, 12e.

Ataxia
Ataxia = impaired coordination, not weakness
• Sensory: impaired proprioceptive → worse with eyes closed; positive Romberg
• Cerebellar: wide-based gait, dysmetria, intention tremor
• Vestibular: vertigo, nystagmus, imbalance

Tabes Dorsalis
• Late manifestation of neurosyphilis
• Degeneration of dorsal columns + dorsal roots
• ↓ Vibration/proprioception → sensory ataxia, positive Romberg
• Dorsal root involvement → absent reflexes + lightning pains
• May cause urinary dysfunction (loss of bladder fullness sensation → dorsal root involvement)
• Argyll Robertson pupils: accommodate but do not react to light
SCD → dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts
Tabes dorsalis → dorsal columns + dorsal roots
Last, 12e.

Friedreich Ataxia
• Autosomal recessive; GAA repeat expansion in frataxin
Degeneration of:
• Dorsal columns → ↓ vibration/proprioception → sensory ataxia
Last, 12e.
• Spinocerebellar tracts → ↓ proprioceptive input to cerebellum → gait/limb ataxia
• Corticospinal tracts → UMN signs (spasticity, Babinski)
• Absent DTRs → impaired sensory afferent limb of reflex arc
• Associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes
• Onset in childhood/adolescence
SCD → dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts
Tabes dorsalis → dorsal columns + dorsal roots
Friedreich → dorsal columns + spinocerebellar + corticospinal tracts

Poliomyelitis
• Poliovirus selectively damages anterior horn motor neurons
• Produces LMN signs
• Flaccid weakness/paralysis
• ↓ Muscle tone
• ↓ Reflexes
• Muscle atrophy
• Sensation is preserved
• Weakness may be asymmetric
Last, 12e.
Anterior horn lesion → LMN signs with preserved sensation

Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA)
• Autosomal recessive disorder due to SMN1 (Survival Motor Neuron 1) gene deletion/mutation
• Degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons
• Produces LMN signs: weakness, hypotonia, muscle atrophy, ↓ reflexes
• Sensation preserved
SMA Type I (Werdnig-Hoffmann Disease)
• Severe infantile form
• “Floppy infant”
• Symmetric proximal weakness
• Tongue fasciculations
• Respiratory weakness may occur
Poliomyelitis: viral destruction of anterior horn cells
SMA: genetic degeneration of anterior horn cells
Both → LMN signs with preserved sensation

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) / Lou Gehrig’s Disease
• Progressive degeneration of:
• Lateral corticospinal tracts (UMN) → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski
• Anterior horn motor neurons (LMN) → weakness, atrophy, fasciculations
• Mixed UMN + LMN signs
• Often begins asymmetrically
• Sensation is preserved
• Bulbar involvement → dysarthria, dysphagia
• Respiratory muscle weakness may occur
Polio → anterior horn → LMN
SMA → anterior horn → LMN
Last, 12e.
ALS → anterior horn + corticospinal tract → LMN + UMN

Conus Medullaris Syndrome (CMS)
• Lesion of the terminal spinal cord (conus medullaris)
• Findings usually bilateral and symmetric
• May produce mixed UMN + LMN signs
• Saddle anesthesia
• Early bladder/bowel dysfunction
• Radicular pain is typically less prominent than in CES
Conus medullaris = spinal cord → may have UMN/LMN signs
Typically symmetric findings + early sphincter dysfunction
Vaishya. World Neurosurg X, 2024

Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES)
• Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris
• LMN signs
• Flaccid weakness
• ↓/absent reflexes
• Sensory loss often asymmetric
• Saddle anesthesia
• Radicular low back/leg pain
• Bladder/bowel dysfunction may occur
Cauda equina = nerve roots
→ asymmetric LMN findings
Vaishya. World Neurosurg X, 2024
Conus = cord → may have UMN + LMN signs; symmetric; early sphincter dysfunction
Cauda equina = roots → LMN only; asymmetric; prominent radicular pain

Complete Spinal Cord Transection
Acute Phase — Spinal Shock
• Loss of motor and sensory function below the lesion
• Flaccid paralysis
• Areflexia
• Loss of autonomic function
• Cervical/high thoracic injury may cause hypotension + bradycardia
After Spinal Shock Resolves
• Spasticity
• Hyperreflexia
• Babinski signs
• Persistent paralysis below the lesion
Acute cord injury → spinal shock: flaccid + areflexic
Later → UMN signs: spastic + hyperreflexic + Babinski

Summary
• Localize: modality + side + level
• UMN: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski
• LMN: flaccidity, hyporeflexia, atrophy/fasciculations
• Tract location + decussation → pattern of deficits
• Selective tract disease → characteristic combinations of deficits
• Cord lesions → UMN ± LMN | Root lesions → LMN
• Spinal shock: acute areflexia/flaccidity → later UMN signs
